name: Selective Attention
description: People attend to only a small subset of the stimuli available to them, usually the ones most relevant to their current goal. Fully visible interface elements can still go unnoticed when attention is already committed elsewhere.
design_relevance_note: Directly relevant to notifications, banners, multi-change screens, onboarding cues, and any situation where something important can be visually present yet still be missed.
myth_risk_note: Selective attention is well-established across neuroscience and psychology, but rated low rather than none because the existing corpus evidence focuses on specific manifestations (inattentional blindness, banner blindness) rather than the full breadth of the principle, and transfer to design contexts remains partially inferred rather than directly measured in UI studies.
prevalence_note: Dedicated Laws of UX entry and regularly invoked through banner-blindness/change-blindness discussions in interface design, but less likely to be named outright than Fitts, Hick, Miller, or cognitive load.

findings.description: In a dynamic-scene selective-attention task, whether observers notice a fully visible, unexpected object depends on how similar that object is to the objects they are already attending to and on how demanding their primary task is — but not on the unexpected object's spatial proximity to the attended region. This supports an object/event-based account of inattentional blindness rather than a purely spatial one: full physical visibility does not guarantee perception when attention is engaged elsewhere.
findings.source_title: Gorillas in Our Midst: Sustained Inattentional Blindness for Dynamic Events

findings.description: In controlled experiments, users frequently overlooked distinctive, highlighted banner links exactly when they were specifically looking for that kind of information — the 'irony' of banner blindness. Banners located higher on the page (further from other content links) were missed more often than those lower down, and banners were missed more when users weren't required to click them to complete a task.
findings.source_title: Banner Blindness: The Irony of Attention Grabbing on the World Wide Web
findings.source_venue: Proceedings of the Human Factors and Ergonomics Society Annual Meeting

applications.title: A Westfield usability-test participant missing a prominent year in a timeline
applications.description: In a usability study, a user trying to find when Westfield entered the UK market read carefully through an entire timeline's body text but failed to notice the year '2000' displayed prominently at the top of the same timeline pop-up -- a direct demonstration of tunnel vision, where focus on one part of a screen causes a user to miss clearly visible information elsewhere.
applications.ethical_note: A pure usability-research finding about how attention narrows during a task, with no persuasion or manipulation angle -- a design lesson about information placement, not a technique used to influence a decision.
